extracted.intended_audience: Montana attorneys, agency staff, hearing examiners, and others who draft or challenge administrative rules and contested-case proceedings under Montana law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on Montana Administrative Procedure Act (MAPA) requirements for agency rulemaking, public inspection, contested-case adjudications, filing/publication of rules, hearing practice, and judicial review in Montana. Includes definitions, procedural checklists, forms, and legislative oversight roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking notice and opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: State agency rulemaking normally be preceded by notice and an opportunity for interested persons to submit views or information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a fundamental principle (ABA resolution). The handbook treats notice-and-comment as a baseline expectation for legitimate rulemaking. Examples and legislative history discuss publication in the Administrative Register/Code and mail polling of legislators as Montana-specific practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rights in adjudicative hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rights in state agency adjudicative hearings be set forth by statute with particularity to secure fairness coupled with efficiency; matters include requirements of adequate notice, rules of evidence, contents of the record, basis for decision, impartiality of the adjudicator, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handbook emphasizes that MAPA should specify these rights; the discussion points to rules of evidence (see section on 'Rules of Evidence'), contents of the record, and requirement that decisions contain findings and bases. Cases (e.g., Burgess v. Softich) illustrate when a hearing is constitutionally required even if statute is silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public inspection of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: State agency rules be published, and other state agency law or policy affecting rights of the public be made available generally for public inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 6.1(c)-(d) requires agencies to make rules and written policies available for inspection and to provide copies on request (agencies may charge copy cost unless statute provides otherwise). The Secretary of State publishes the Administrative Code/Register; agencies must file rules in accordance with filing statutes (see cross-references to 82-4205/4206).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must adopt rules describing organization and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency shall adopt as a rule a description of its organization (course and method of operations and methods whereby the public may obtain information or make submissions or requests) and adopt rules of practice setting forth the nature and requirements of all formal and informal procedures available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice and hearing requirements of 82-4204 do not apply to adoption of a rule describing organization. Subsection (1)(b) requires procedural rules, forms, and instructions be set out so the public and agency personnel have guidance and agency procedures are stabilized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate judicial review of agency action be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an ABA principle. The handbook later details petition for judicial review (forms, grounds, procedures) and standards (e.g., clearly erroneous, arbitrary and capricious). See sections on filing petition, responses, grounds for review, and appeals to the Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'agency' and statutory exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Agency' means any agency of the state government authorized to make rules, determine contested cases, or enter into contracts, except specified exemptions (e.g., board of pardons (partially), supervision/administration of penal institutions, board of regents and Montana university system, financing/construction/maintenance of public works, legislative and judicial branches, governor's office, military/civil defense agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handbook reproduces R.C.M. 82-4202(1) and explains derivation/purpose and reasons for exemptions (practicality, constitutional rights, federal-aid concerns). It notes the 1977 amendment narrowing/adjusting exemptions and explains the use of a reference to 82-4227 for some exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'rule' (broad substantive definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rule' means each agency regulation, standard, or statement of general applicability that implements, interprets, or prescribes law or policy or describes organization, procedures, or practice requirements of an agency; includes amendment or repeal of a prior rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition distinguishes substantive rules as either legislative (force of law when adopted in accordance) or interpretive/adjective (may codify an interpretation but lack force of law). The handbook cautions the breadth of 'rule' may initially impose burdens on agencies and gives examples (contested-case decisions becoming precedent; state plans interpreting federal law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from the definition of 'rule'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'rule' does not include: (a) statements concerning only internal management not affecting private rights; (b) declaratory rulings under 82-4218; (c) rules relating to use of public works/facilities when substance is indicated by signs/signals; (d) seasonal rules adopted annually for hunting/fishing/trapping when statute requires publication and certain recreational rules indicated by signs; (e) rules implementing state personnel classification, wage/salary plan, statewide budgeting/accounting; (f) uniform rules under interstate compact (though these must be filed and published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific statutory exemptions were locally developed and are intended to avoid impractical burdens (e.g., speed limits, fish/game rules often adopted on short notice). The handbook explains the policy reasons for each exemption and notes the 1977 amendment changes (e.g., personnel/budgeting language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive vs legislative rules (force and filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive rules are either legislative rules (if adopted in accordance with this part and under expressly delegated authority, have the force of law) or interpretive/adjective rules (which may be adopted to codify an interpretation and lack force of law). Filing of interpretive rules is optional under the 1977 amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses debate among agencies about codifying interpretations: decentralized programs often file interpretations for uniform administration, while centralized programs seldom file. The distinction affects whether a rule has legal force and whether filing is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'contested case'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Contested case' means any proceeding before an agency in which a determination of legal rights, duties, or privileges of a party is required by law to be made after an opportunity for hearing; includes but is not restricted to rate-making, price fixing, and licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition is broad: 'required by law' includes constitutional due-process requirements (a hearing may be required even absent statutory provision). It is not intended to include informal preliminary inquiries or investigations. Case law examples illustrate the contours (e.g., Burgess v. Softich required a hearing despite lack of statutory provision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of 'license', 'licensing', 'person', and 'party'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'License' includes any agency permit, certificate, approval, registration, charter, or other permission required by law but not a license required solely for revenue purposes. 'Licensing' includes agency processes respecting grant, denial, renewal, revocation, suspension, annulment, withdrawal, limitation, transfer, or amendment of a license. 'Party' means any person or agency named or admitted as a party or entitled as of right to be admitted; 'person' means individual, partnership, corporation, association, governmental subdivision, or public organization other than an agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handbook notes additions to the Model Act (e.g., inclusion of 'renewal', 'transfer') to cover license-as-property transactions and explains the 'solely for revenue purposes' exemption intends to exclude purely ministerial revenue licences. The 'party' provision permits agencies to admit interested persons for limited purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public inspection requirement and effect of noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency must make available for public inspection all rules and written statements of policy or interpretations used in discharge of its functions; upon request, provide copies (may charge cost). No agency rule is valid or effective against any person or party whose rights have been substantially prejudiced by an agency's failure to comply with the public inspection requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is R.C.M. 82-4203(1)(c)-(d) and (2). The handbook stresses that lack of published procedures creates uncertainty for litigants and that compliance corrects serious administrative deficiencies. The invalidity remedy protects prejudiced persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must adopt procedural rules of practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must adopt rules of practice, not inconsistent with statute, setting forth the nature and requirements of all formal and informal procedures available, including descriptions of all forms and instructions used by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to correct lack of public information and to stabilize agency procedures. The handbook comments that some agencies mistakenly believe they lack authority to adopt such rules; MAPA requires them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing examiner pre-hearing preparation duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearing examiner should review MAPA and relevant statutes and agency rules; review pleadings; order pre-hearing conferences to determine agreed and contested facts and issues; write pre-hearing order governing place/time/conduct of hearing and schedule for preliminary motions; entertain and rule on pre-hearing motions; remember ex parte consultation restrictions; observe open meetings and public participation requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form 21 (Hearing Examiner's Checklist) supplies detailed step-by-step prehearing tasks. The handbook highlights the need to explain statutory provisions and rules to unrepresented parties and to set schedules for motions and filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing examiner conduct of hearing duties
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting the hearing the examiner should call the hearing to order, identify case, introduce self and agency members, explain authority and statutory/rule provisions for the hearing, explain order of presentation, afford opportunity for opening statements, manage direct and cross-examination, swear witnesses, mark exhibits, allow rebuttal and surrebuttal, permit questions from agency members, control decorum, ensure only one person speaks at a time, and take sufficient notes to make findings and recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form 21 outlines order and details for opening, presentation, evidence handling, and control. Examiner should ensure procedural fairness, explain rights (e.g., right to counsel), and manage time and record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing examiner post-hearing duties
rubrics_metrics.description: After hearing, order proposed findings of fact, conclusions of law, and briefs from parties with a set schedule; explain statutory authority and role of the hearing examiner in final agency decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form 21 IV emphasizes post-hearing scheduling, the examiner's obligation to produce recommended findings, and clarifying the weight of the examiner's recommendation to agency decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of notice of hearing / proposed suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of proposed suspension (example Form 14) must state the time/place of hearing, statutory and rule authority for the action, the alleged violations (specific rule citations and factual allegations), and inform the respondent they are entitled to attend, present evidence and argument, have counsel, and that they must notify the agency within a statutory period (e.g., fifteen days) to contest or the action may proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms show how to draft clear notices: include authority citations (statute and ARM), factual allegation(s) with dates/times, nature of relief proposed (e.g., suspension duration), and instructions for asserting a request for hearing and deadlines. Amended notices may supply more definite statements when requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for hearing and more definite statement procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may file a request for hearing and application for a more definite statement specifying missing particulars (e.g., citation and section allegedly violated, time of alleged violation, term of proposed sanction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form 15 demonstrates that agencies should respond by amending notices to provide requested specifics (see Form 16 amended notice) to ensure hearings focus on identified issues and allow for fair preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of petition for declaratory ruling
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for declaratory ruling (Form 19) should include petitioner's name/address, facts presented, rules involved (identify codes/sections), question presented, petitioner's contention, ruling requested, and identification of known interested persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form 19 provides a template for requests seeking agency interpretation of rules (e.g., application of Life Safety Code). The handbook discusses when declaratory rulings are appropriate vs contested cases and cross-references MAPA provisions on declaratory rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and Administrative Code Committee roles in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators and the Administrative Code Committee have roles including introducing joint resolutions to repeal/amend/compel adoption of a rule; polling all members on consistency of proposed rule with legislative intent; reviewing proposed rules and submitting recommendations; requiring public hearings; shifting burden of proof in later challenges; determining Register publication frequency; and advising on filing/publication fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form 20 (Checklist of Legislative Roles) details individual member powers during session and interim and Committee powers at any time. The handbook notes Montana-specific procedures (mail polling of all legislators) and that the Committee can affect litigation posture by documenting legislative intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of forms/templates for contested cases and judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The handbook provides model forms for notices, requests for hearing, amended notices, motions (e.g., motion for summary decision), consent orders, petitions for judicial review, and other pleadings; forms include suggested content, procedural notes, and illustrative language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix forms are distilled from agency files and intended as practical templates. Notes warn that local agency rules or statutes may require variations and that economic loss to competitors is likely not grounds to deny certain licenses (illustrative legal note in form 13).
